<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract.</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">The emergence of large-scale Mixture of Experts (MoE) models represents a significant advancement in artificial intelligence, offering enhanced model capacity and computational efficiency through conditional computation. However, deploying and running inference on these models presents significant challenges in computational resources, latency, and energy efficiency. This comprehensive survey analyzes optimization techniques for MoE models across the entire system stack.
We first establish a taxonomical framework that categorizes optimization approaches into model-level, system-level, and hardware-level optimizations. At the model level, we examine architectural innovations including efficient expert design, attention mechanisms, various compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation, as well as algorithm improvement including dynamic routing strategies and expert merging methods. At the system level, we investigate distributed computing approaches, load balancing mechanisms, and efficient scheduling algorithms that enable scalable deployment. Furthermore, we delve into hardware-specific optimizations and co-design strategies that maximize throughput and energy efficiency.
This survey provides both a structured overview of existing solutions and identifies key challenges and promising research directions in MoE inference optimization.
To facilitate ongoing updates and the sharing of cutting-edge advances in MoE
inference optimization research, we have established a repository accessible at <a href="https://github.com/MoE-Inf/awesome-moe-inference/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/MoE-Inf/awesome-moe-inference/</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Mixture of Experts, Large Language Models, Inference Optimization
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1. </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized artificial intelligence, demonstrating unprecedented capabilities across various domains including natural language processing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib181" title="" class="ltx_ref">181</a>, <a href="#bib.bib128" title="" class="ltx_ref">128</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>)</cite>, computer vision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib222" title="" class="ltx_ref">222</a>)</cite>, and multimodal tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib136" title="" class="ltx_ref">136</a>, <a href="#bib.bib92" title="" class="ltx_ref">92</a>, <a href="#bib.bib187" title="" class="ltx_ref">187</a>)</cite>. Models like GPT-4 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib127" title="" class="ltx_ref">127</a>)</cite>, Claude <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>)</cite>, and Gemini <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib175" title="" class="ltx_ref">175</a>)</cite> have achieved remarkable performance in tasks ranging from natural language understanding to complex reasoning and code generation. The impressive capabilities of these models are largely attributed to their massive scale, both in terms of model parameters and computational resources invested in training. This scaling trend is supported by empirical evidence showing consistent improvements in model performance with increased size, as demonstrated by various scaling laws in language modeling and other domains <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">78</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>)</cite>. However, this trajectory presents significant challenges in terms of computational efficiency and resource utilization, particularly during inference, where real-world deployment constraints become critical <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib230" title="" class="ltx_ref">230</a>, <a href="#bib.bib198" title="" class="ltx_ref">198</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib215" title="" class="ltx_ref">215</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Mixture of Experts (MoE) has emerged as a promising architectural solution to address scaling challenges in machine learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib156" title="" class="ltx_ref">156</a>)</cite>. Originally introduced by Jacobs et al.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>)</cite> in the early 1990s as a method for learning subtasks in neural networks. Numerous MoE-based models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>, <a href="#bib.bib179" title="" class="ltx_ref">179</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>)</cite> have been developed over the years. In the era of large language models, MoE has again experienced a renaissance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib171" title="" class="ltx_ref">171</a>)</cite>. The core principle of MoE is to distribute the model’s capacity across multiple specialized sub-networks, or experts, with a learned routing mechanism that selectively activates only the relevant experts for each input. This approach allows models to maintain a large parameter count while keeping computational costs manageable through sparse activation. Recent implementations, such as Mixtral 8x7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>)</cite>, DeepSeek-V3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>)</cite> and DBRX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib178" title="" class="ltx_ref">178</a>)</cite>, have demonstrated the effectiveness of this strategy in scaling language models to trillions of parameters while maintaining reasonable computational requirements.</p>
</div>

<tr id="S1.T1.3.2" class="ltx_tr">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S1.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>. </span><span id="S1.T1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">A List of SoTA MoEs. Param. represents the number of total parameters. Experts are listed according to the format of the number of activation experts, total experts, and shared experts. #L represents the number of hidden layers, #H represents the number of attention heads. <math id="S1.T1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{model}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{model}</annotation></semantics></math> is the hidden size, <math id="S1.T1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{ffn}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{ffn}</annotation></semantics></math> is the intermediate size of FFNs, <math id="S1.T1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{expert}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{expert}</annotation></semantics></math> is the intermediate size of FFN experts.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_ERROR ltx_centering">{forest}</span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>. </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Taxonomy of MoE inference optimization.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The success of MoE in scaling models has led to its adoption in various state-of-the-art systems. For example, Google’s GLaM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>)</cite> outperforms GPT-3 while using significantly fewer computational resources during inference. Similarly, Mixtral 8x7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>)</cite> has demonstrated competitive performance compared to much larger dense models, while maintaining efficient inference characteristics.
DeepSeek-V3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>)</cite>, a recent open-source MoE model,
has surpassed other open-source alternatives and demonstrated performance comparable to prominent closed-source models such as GPT4-o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet.
Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes recent state-of-the-art open-source MoE models that have garnered significant attention, showcasing their rapid evolution and widespread adoption across major tech companies and research institutions. The models range in size from 6.7B to 671B parameters, with varying architectures characterized by different numbers of experts, hidden layers, and attention heads. The chronological progression from 2022 to late 2024 demonstrates increasing model sizes and architectural sophistication, with recent models like DeepSeek-V3 pushing the boundaries in terms of parameter count and model performance. This trend further highlights the strong potential of the MoE architecture in advancing the field of large language models.
These successes have sparked widespread interest in MoE across both academia and industry, leading to innovations in model design <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib189" title="" class="ltx_ref">189</a>, <a href="#bib.bib220" title="" class="ltx_ref">220</a>)</cite>, training techniques <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib108" title="" class="ltx_ref">108</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>)</cite>, and deployment strategies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib210" title="" class="ltx_ref">210</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">However, the efficient deployment of MoE models for inference presents unique and significant challenges <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib173" title="" class="ltx_ref">173</a>, <a href="#bib.bib208" title="" class="ltx_ref">208</a>, <a href="#bib.bib226" title="" class="ltx_ref">226</a>, <a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>)</cite>. The dynamic nature of expert activation patterns introduces complexity in resource management and scheduling that is not present in traditional dense models.
At the model level, the design of efficient expert architectures faces challenges in balancing model capacity with computational efficiency, while routing mechanisms must optimize expert selection and load distribution.
The system-level challenges are particularly complex: distributed computation requires sophisticated scheduling algorithms to manage expert placement and activation, load balancing must handle dynamic workload variations across experts, and memory management needs to efficiently handle the loading and unloading of expert parameters.
Hardware-level challenges stem from the fundamental mismatch between traditional hardware architectures optimized for dense computation and the sparse, dynamic nature of MoE inference. This necessitates specialized acceleration techniques to handle sparse computation patterns, manage memory bandwidth efficiently, and provide flexible computation capabilities for dynamic expert switching. Communication overhead in distributed settings presents another significant challenge, particularly when experts are distributed across different devices or nodes, requiring careful optimization of data movement and synchronization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Numerous methods have been developed to address these challenges in MoE deployment and inference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">76</a>, <a href="#bib.bib195" title="" class="ltx_ref">195</a>, <a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">139</a>, <a href="#bib.bib152" title="" class="ltx_ref">152</a>)</cite>. While the rapid growth of research in this field demonstrates its importance, it can also make it difficult to identify key trends and best practices. A critical gap in the existing literature is the absence of a systematic framework for analyzing and developing comprehensive inference optimization solutions for MoE models.
To bridge this gap, our work offers a comprehensive survey of inference optimization techniques for MoE models. We propose a taxonomical framework that categorizes optimization approaches into model-level, system-level, and hardware-level optimizations, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. This framework provides a structured approach to understanding and comparing different optimization techniques. While there are related surveys on LLM efficiency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib215" title="" class="ltx_ref">215</a>, <a href="#bib.bib90" title="" class="ltx_ref">90</a>, <a href="#bib.bib96" title="" class="ltx_ref">96</a>, <a href="#bib.bib180" title="" class="ltx_ref">180</a>, <a href="#bib.bib183" title="" class="ltx_ref">183</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib230" title="" class="ltx_ref">230</a>, <a href="#bib.bib198" title="" class="ltx_ref">198</a>)</cite> and MoE architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib182" title="" class="ltx_ref">182</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>)</cite>, our work is the first to specifically focus on inference optimization techniques for MoE models. We systematically analyze optimization approaches at different abstraction levels, from model architecture to hardware acceleration, providing a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners working deploy MoE models for different real-world applications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The remainder of this survey is organized as follows: Section <a href="#S2" title="2. Fundamentals of Mixture of Experts ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> provides background on MoE models and their inference characteristics. Sections 3-5 detail optimization techniques at the model, system, and hardware levels respectively. Section <a href="#S6" title="6. Future Directions and Open Challenges ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> discusses future challenges and opportunities, and Section <a href="#S7" title="7. Conclusion ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> concludes the survey.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2. </span>Fundamentals of Mixture of Experts</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MoE represents a significant architectural paradigm in neural networks, particularly in large language models, where it enables conditional computation through sparse activation mechanisms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>)</cite>. At its core, an MoE architecture consists of a routing network <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(x)</annotation></semantics></math> and a set of expert networks <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{E_{1},E_{2},...,E_{N}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{E_{1},E_{2},...,E_{N}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the total number of experts. The fundamental principle of MoE can be expressed as <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=\sum_{i=1}^{N}g_{i}(x)\cdot E_{i}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=\sum_{i=1}^{N}g_{i}(x)\cdot E_{i}(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{i}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{i}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> represents the gating function for expert <math id="S2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{i}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{i}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> is the output of expert <math id="S2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, existing studies typically use the MoE module to replace part of the traditional dense layer, thereby forming a sparse MoE layer. While most research focuses on substituting the FFN module with the MoE module <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib177" title="" class="ltx_ref">177</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>)</cite>, some have also explored replacing the Attention module <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib158" title="" class="ltx_ref">158</a>, <a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">76</a>, <a href="#bib.bib159" title="" class="ltx_ref">159</a>, <a href="#bib.bib220" title="" class="ltx_ref">220</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The typical MoE model inference procedure follows a sequence of expert selection, parallel computation, and output aggregation.
First, the router computes expert selection probabilities:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(1)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=\text{Softmax}(R(x))" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>Softmax</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=\text{Softmax}(R(x))</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> is the input token embedding, <math id="S2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is the routing function, and <math id="S2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the expert selection probabilities for <math id="S2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> total experts.
Next, the top-k experts are selected based on these probabilities:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(2)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\text{selected}}=\text{TopK}(\theta,K)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>selected</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>TopK</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\text{selected}}=\text{TopK}(\theta,K)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\text{selected}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>selected</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\text{selected}}</annotation></semantics></math> contains the indices of the K selected experts, <math id="S2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\leq N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\leq N</annotation></semantics></math>.
The selected experts then process the input in parallel:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(3)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}=E_{i}(x),\quad\forall i\in E_{\text{selected}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>selected</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}=E_{i}(x),\quad\forall i\in E_{\text{selected}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{i}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{i}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> represents the computation of expert <math id="S2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is its output.
Finally, the expert outputs are combined through weighted aggregation:</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(4)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=\sum_{i\in E_{\text{selected}}}\frac{\theta_{i}}{\sum_{j\in E_{\text{selected}}}\theta_{j}}\cdot y_{i}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>selected</mtext></msub></mrow></munder><mfrac><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>selected</mtext></msub></mrow></msub><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=\sum_{i\in E_{\text{selected}}}\frac{\theta_{i}}{\sum_{j\in E_{\text{selected}}}\theta_{j}}\cdot y_{i}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The MoE architecture offers several compelling advantages that have contributed to its growing adoption in modern neural networks. First, the conditional computation mechanism enables significant computational savings compared to dense models of similar capacity. By activating only a subset of experts for each input token, MoE models can process information more efficiently while maintaining high performance levels. This is particularly valuable in resource-constrained environments or when scaling to larger model sizes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Second, the specialization of individual experts allows for more nuanced and accurate processing of different input patterns. Each expert can develop specialized knowledge for specific aspects of the input space, leading to more refined and targeted computations. This specialization is particularly beneficial in language models, where different experts can focus on various linguistic patterns, domains, or tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Third, the dynamic routing mechanism enables adaptive computation based on input complexity. More challenging or nuanced inputs can engage multiple experts with complementary specializations, while simpler inputs might require only a small subset of experts. This adaptive resource allocation helps optimize the computation-performance trade-off and potentially improves both efficiency and effectiveness.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p10.1" class="ltx_p">By partitioning dense models into relatively independent expert models and dynamically activating specific subsets (or the entire set) of experts based on each input token, the model’s overall performance can be significantly enhanced with only a marginal increase in inference computation. This approach clearly demonstrates the MoE model’s exceptional flexibility and scalability.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3. </span>Model-level Optimizations</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Model-level optimizations aim to enhance the inherent structure and efficiency of MoE models through systematic improvements in architecture, parameter optimization, and algorithmic design. These optimizations can be broadly categorized into three main areas: efficient model architecture design, model compression techniques, and algorithmic improvements. Architecture design focuses on developing more efficient expert and attention structures, while compression techniques aim to reduce model size and memory footprint through methods such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation. Algorithmic improvements concentrate on enhancing the dynamic aspects of MoE models, including routing mechanisms and expert combination strategies. Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3. Model-level Optimizations ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> illustrates the detailed taxonomy of model-level optimization that is described in this section.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_ERROR ltx_centering">{forest}</span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>. </span><span id="S3.F3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Model-level inference optimization techniques for MoE.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1. </span>Efficient Model Architecture Design</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A transformer block typically consists of two main components: the attention module and the
FFN module. To build better MoE models, many studies focus on designing improved versions of both the attention and FFN modules, aiming to achieve strong performance while maintaining high efficiency.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.1. </span>MoE-based Attention Design</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to the typical application of the MoE structure in the FFN module of the transformer layer, current studies explore how to incorporate MoE into the Attention module for improved performance. MAE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib134" title="" class="ltx_ref">134</a>)</cite> was the first to explain the multi-head attention mechanism from the MoE perspective, using a learned gating function to activate different experts for different inputs, with each expert consisting of <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n-1</annotation></semantics></math> heads. To further optimize MoE-based attention modules, existing research proposes various structures. MoA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib220" title="" class="ltx_ref">220</a>)</cite> and BAM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib218" title="" class="ltx_ref">218</a>)</cite> select <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> heads for a given input and share key projection and value projection weights among all heads, while SwitchHead <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>)</cite> shares key projection and query projection weights to enhance computational efficiency. MoH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">76</a>)</cite> introduces shared heads and a two-stage routing process to further improve the standard MoE method, offering an advantage over MoA. Building upon MoA, ModuleFormer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib159" title="" class="ltx_ref">159</a>)</cite> extends sparse modules to both the attention and feed-forward layers, allowing for the easy addition and removal of modules. Inspired by MoA and ModuleFormer, JetMoE-8B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib158" title="" class="ltx_ref">158</a>)</cite> develops a powerful open-source model featuring sparse attention and sparse feed-forward layers, while DS-MoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib130" title="" class="ltx_ref">130</a>)</cite> proposes a hybrid dense training and sparse inference framework for efficient training and inference. Additionally, SUT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib172" title="" class="ltx_ref">172</a>)</cite> and MoEUT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>)</cite> use sparse attention and sparse feed-forward layers to construct the efficient Sparse Universal Transformer model, which shares parameters across all layers.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.2. </span>MoE-based FFN Design</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To enhance the efficiency of MoE-based models, current research explores various variants of the standard MoE module. MoE++ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>)</cite> introduces three types of zero-computation experts based on standard experts, aimed at reducing computational overhead. SCoMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib196" title="" class="ltx_ref">196</a>)</cite> leverages a structured all-to-all communication approach, inspired by hierarchical communication topologies, to reduce communication costs during parallel MoE computation. Pre-gated MoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>)</cite> proposes a pre-gated MoE module that prefetches the required experts to improve inference speed on memory-constrained devices. COMET <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>)</cite> introduces a tree-based sparse expert selection mechanism to optimize the traditional gating module, which typically relies on a linear approach. Additionally, MoELoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib113" title="" class="ltx_ref">113</a>)</cite> reimagines LoRA as a MoE for more parameter-efficient fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2. </span>Model Compression Techniques</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Model compression is a popular area of research for reducing model size in current LLM studies, with techniques such as pruning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib116" title="" class="ltx_ref">116</a>, <a href="#bib.bib100" title="" class="ltx_ref">100</a>)</cite>, quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib185" title="" class="ltx_ref">185</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>)</cite>, knowledge distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>)</cite>, and low-rank decomposition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib190" title="" class="ltx_ref">190</a>, <a href="#bib.bib214" title="" class="ltx_ref">214</a>)</cite>. Since experts constitute the majority of the weights in MoE models (e.g., 96% for Mixtral-8x7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>)</cite>), most MoE-related compression efforts focus on applying these common techniques specifically to the experts.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F4.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2412.14219v2/figures/pruning.png" id="S3.F4.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:238/151;" width="238" height="151" alt="Refer to caption">

<td id="S3.T2.3.14.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r"><span id="S3.T2.3.14.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">MoE-compression <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>)</cite></span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.3.14.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r"><span id="S3.T2.3.14.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">50%</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.3.14.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r"><span id="S3.T2.3.14.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">A</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.3.14.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r"><span id="S3.T2.3.14.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Lima <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib227" title="" class="ltx_ref">227</a>)</cite> MetaMathQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib211" title="" class="ltx_ref">211</a>)</cite></span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.3.14.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b"><span id="S3.T2.3.14.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">✓</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.3.14.6" class="ltx_td ltx_border_b ltx_border_r"></td>
<td id="S3.T2.3.14.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b"><span id="S3.T2.3.14.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">✓</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2. </span>A comparison of pruning methods. Sparsity indicates the max ratio of pruning. TSA represents task specific or agnostic. EEP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib104" title="" class="ltx_ref">104</a>)</cite> does not require additional fine-tuning. Finetuning datasets of MS-SMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib99" title="" class="ltx_ref">99</a>)</cite> are SST2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib166" title="" class="ltx_ref">166</a>)</cite> MRPC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>)</cite> MultiRC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>)</cite> COPA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib147" title="" class="ltx_ref">147</a>)</cite> WinoGrande <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib150" title="" class="ltx_ref">150</a>)</cite> SQuAD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib141" title="" class="ltx_ref">141</a>)</cite> WikiQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib205" title="" class="ltx_ref">205</a>)</cite>and HotpotQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib206" title="" class="ltx_ref">206</a>)</cite>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to the large number of parameters in MoE-based models, current research explores pruning methods to reduce the number of parameters in MoE experts. These methods are generally divided into structured and unstructured pruning. Most studies focus on structured expert pruning, which aims to reduce the number of experts in the MoE layer while maintaining model accuracy. As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.2. Model Compression Techniques ‣ 3. Model-level Optimizations ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>-(a), some approaches directly remove unimportant experts (left side), while others merge groups of experts into a single expert (right side). TSEP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>)</cite> removes non-professional experts for the target downstream task while fine-tuning professional experts to preserve model performance. They also demonstrate the superiority of the eager expert pruning paradigm over other possible solutions like two-pass optimization or staged expert pruning. NAEE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib112" title="" class="ltx_ref">112</a>)</cite> eliminates unimportant experts by evaluating expert combinations on a small calibration dataset to minimize accuracy loss, simultaneously reduce model sizes and increase inference speed. while UNCURL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib153" title="" class="ltx_ref">153</a>)</cite> reduces the number of experts based on MoE router logits. Some insights useful to model design choices considering task-specific inference optimization can give guidance for later stages. PEMPE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>)</cite> prunes experts that have smaller changes in the router’s <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm between the pre-trained and fine-tuned models, and will conduct experiments with other compression techniques on SOTA vision MoEs. SEER-MoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib120" title="" class="ltx_ref">120</a>)</cite> employs a heavy-hitters counting method for expert pruning, then with regularization-based fine-tuning reaches further expert pruning. MoE-<math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>I</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib203" title="" class="ltx_ref">203</a>)</cite> proposes the Layer-wise Genetic Search and Block-wise KT-Reception Field with the non-uniform pruning ratio to prune unimportant experts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to direct pruning, some studies utilize expert merging to reduce the number of experts. For unstructured pruning, MoE-Pruner <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib195" title="" class="ltx_ref">195</a>)</cite> prunes weights with the smallest magnitudes, weighted by the corresponding input activations and router weights. The pruned MoE models can benefit from a pre-trained teacher model through expert-wise knowledge distillation and have compatibility with structured pruning. Moreover, STUN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">87</a>)</cite> combines structured and unstructured pruning to achieve better performance than unstructured pruning alone, utilizing the sparse character of MoEs based on behavior similarity in a greedy manner. MoE-Compression <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>)</cite> proposes a unified framework for MoE compression, using both structured and unstructured pruning methods to achieve significant inference speedup with minimal accuracy loss.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Another potential approach is merging outdated experts based on their parameters to achieve better performance. Branch-Train-Merge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib97" title="" class="ltx_ref">97</a>)</cite> independently trains different parts of the model on distinct subsets of data, eliminating the need for large-scale multi-node synchronization typically required in traditional LLM training. Building on this, Branch-Train-Mix <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib169" title="" class="ltx_ref">169</a>)</cite> trains multiple copies of a seed LLM to specialize in multiple domains in an asynchronous and parallel fashion, then merges the parameters of the MoE layer to create a unified model that can be further trained. The second finetuning stage makes the final LLM more performant. They also find that their approach is more computing efficient compared to the dense model or specialized MoE model on training. Park et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib133" title="" class="ltx_ref">133</a>)</cite> observed that introducing a shared layer in the MoE could lead to performance degradation. To address this, they trained merged experts that learned the same features in different ways, improving their ability to generalize and mitigating catastrophic forgetting during incremental learning of multi-domain tasks. MC-SMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib99" title="" class="ltx_ref">99</a>)</cite> divides experts into different groups based on routing policies and then merges each group into one expert. HC-SMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>)</cite> is a framework that uses hierarchical clustering to merge experts without requiring retraining and can be applied in a task-agnostic manner. During inference, MEO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>)</cite> systematically investigates the computational cost of MoE. In the drop-in replacement algorithm, they first merge the selected expert parameters and then perform efficient computation. FoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib186" title="" class="ltx_ref">186</a>)</cite> fuses the outputs of expert models by leveraging their complementary knowledge of the data distribution, framing it as a supervised learning instance. DEK <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib221" title="" class="ltx_ref">221</a>)</cite> identifies and groups similar experts in feature space, then merges experts within the same group in weight space to reduce the expert count. EEP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib104" title="" class="ltx_ref">104</a>)</cite> introduces a two-stage approach to both prune and merge experts, reducing the total number of experts (saving GPU memory) and the number of active experts (accelerating inference). Inspired by the concept of knowledge transfer in multi-task learning, HyperMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib224" title="" class="ltx_ref">224</a>)</cite> proposes a novel expert network that further increases sparsity while utilizing information from unselected experts as supplementary input. In practice, they capture the contextual information of experts to compensate for the performance loss of transferring knowledge to specific experts. LiteMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib233" title="" class="ltx_ref">233</a>)</cite> retains the most critical experts based on the application’s characteristics, merges secondary experts, and obtains the final sparse model without retraining. This approach enables efficient deployment of lightweight submodels on resource-constrained mobile devices.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">

<td id="S3.T3.3.10.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r">✓</td>
<td id="S3.T3.3.10.3" class="ltx_td ltx_border_b ltx_border_r"></td>
<td id="S3.T3.3.10.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r">1.05x <math id="S3.T3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math> 1.18x</td>
<td id="S3.T3.3.10.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r">5%</td>
<td id="S3.T3.3.10.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r">1.11x <math id="S3.T3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math> 2.78x</td>
<td id="S3.T3.3.10.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b">2, 4, 8</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>. </span><span id="S3.T3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">A comparison of quantization methods.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to model pruning, quantization is an effective technique for reducing model size by converting high-precision weights into low-precision. Given the redundancy of experts in MoE models, current research primarily focuses on quantizing the weights of the experts in MoE. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.2. Model Compression Techniques ‣ 3. Model-level Optimizations ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>-(b), experts are quantized into appropriate low-precision versions using various methods. MC-MoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>)</cite> leverages the access frequency and activation weight to assess the importance of each expert. Along with the associated quantization loss, these metrics are used to determine the optimal quantization configuration for experts via the Integer Programming model. Specifically, the <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th expert’s access frequency is defined as <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{i}=\frac{n_{i}}{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{i}=\frac{n_{i}}{N}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the activation weight is defined as <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{i}=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sigma_{j}}{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><msubsup><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></mstyle><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{i}=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sigma_{j}}{N}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the usage frequency, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> is the routing weight, and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> represents the size of the calibration dataset. The quantization loss, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math> (computed using the Frobenius norm), is then determined for quantizing expert <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> bits (<math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j\in{1,2,3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j\in{1,2,3}</annotation></semantics></math>). Using these metrics, MC-MoE defines the objective function as <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{3}\phi_{i}^{\alpha}\cdot w_{i}^{\beta}\cdot(\epsilon_{ij}\cdot x_{ij})^{\gamma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mrow><msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></msubsup><mrow><msubsup><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>α</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>β</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>γ</mi></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{3}\phi_{i}^{\alpha}\cdot w_{i}^{\beta}\cdot(\epsilon_{ij}\cdot x_{ij})^{\gamma}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is minimized using Integer Programming to determine the optimal bit-width for each expert. MoE-CSP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">83</a>)</cite> quantizes expert weights to either 4 or 8 bits to reduce memory consumption in MoE models. Additionally, it designs specific CUDA kernels that handle the 4-bit/8-bit quantized weights and perform floating-point calculations to accelerate computations. MoQE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">82</a>)</cite> quantizes expert weights to 2 bits to address the memory and latency challenges of MoE models based on its observations that quantizing expert FFN layers to 2 bits does not significantly affect model quality, while quantizing other components, like self-attention, significantly hurts performance. Further advancements include QMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>)</cite> and CMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib213" title="" class="ltx_ref">213</a>)</cite>, which aggressively compress MoE model into just 1 bit. QMoE implements a highly scalable compression algorithm for large models and introduces a custom compression format along with bespoke GPU kernels for efficient on-the-fly computation. On the other hand, CMoE uses binary-weight networks to quantize model weights to 1 bit and applies learned step-size quantization to activations, quantizing them to 4 bits for MoE-based ASR models, enabling deployment on embedded devices. Moreover, some MoE-optimized systems leverage quantization for better system efficiency. MoE-MPTQS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>)</cite> and HOBBIT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib173" title="" class="ltx_ref">173</a>)</cite> dynamically select quantized experts to replace original experts based on the current inputs, thereby reducing the expert loading cost on memory-limited devices. EdgeMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib208" title="" class="ltx_ref">208</a>)</cite> statistically determines the appropriate expert bit-width by profiling expert importance on a calibration dataset. Furthermore, QMoE-Benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib98" title="" class="ltx_ref">98</a>)</cite> provides a benchmark for exploring various MoE structure-aware quantization heuristics, from coarse to fine granularity. The study reveals that different MoE structures (e.g., blocks, experts, linear layers) require different numbers of weight bits for effective and efficient quantization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We summarize the main results reported by the methods discussed above in Table <a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 3.2.2. Expert Quantization ‣ 3.2. Model Compression Techniques ‣ 3. Model-level Optimizations ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. From the table, we observe that quantization primarily benefits memory reduction, with most methods achieving more than a 4x reduction in memory usage. Some methods also lead to actual inference speedup, while others do not. For instance, QMoE even incurs a 5% overhead due to the absence of a dedicated 1-bit inference CUDA kernel implementation and hardware support. Furthermore, quantization typically causes some accuracy loss, with lower bit widths resulting in greater accuracy degradation. Therefore, when applying quantization to a model, it is crucial to strike a balance between memory consumption, accuracy, and inference speedup, taking into account the specific requirements and available hardware resources.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.3. </span>Expert Distillation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Knowledge distillation is another effective method for creating smaller, yet powerful models from larger ones. As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.2. Model Compression Techniques ‣ 3. Model-level Optimizations ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>-(c), knowledge distillation presents a promising solution to generate a compact, high-performance model from the original MoE model.
LLaVA-MoD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib163" title="" class="ltx_ref">163</a>)</cite> combines the MoE structure with knowledge distillation to efficiently train small multimodal large language models (s-MLLMs) from large ones (l-MLLMs). It first incorporates the MoE structure into the s-MLLM to balance computational efficiency and model performance. Then, it introduces two consecutive distillation stages, mimic distillation and preference distillation, to train the s-MLLM. Mimic distillation minimizes the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the output distributions of the s-MLLM and l-MLLM, enabling the s-MLLM to emulate the l-MLLM’s understanding. Preference distillation further refines the s-MLLM using Preference Optimization with additional datasets.
DeepSpeed-MoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">139</a>)</cite> employs staged knowledge distillation to create a distilled version of its proposed PR-MoE model, called MoS. This method reduces model size while maintaining performance. Additionally, some studies focus on transferring the power of sparse models to dense models through knowledge distillation for more efficient deployment. For example, OneS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib199" title="" class="ltx_ref">199</a>)</cite> generates a dense model from a MoE model in two steps: knowledge gathering and knowledge distillation. Knowledge gathering merges experts into a single expert using four aggregation methods, including summation, averaging, top-k knowledge gathering, and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) knowledge gathering. In the second step, knowledge distillation distills the merged model using the original MoE model.
What’s more, MoE-KD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib151" title="" class="ltx_ref">151</a>)</cite> and CMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib213" title="" class="ltx_ref">213</a>)</cite> distill MoE-based speech recognition models into dense models, accelerating the speech recognition process. Specifically, MoE-KD initializes the FFN module of the student dense model with the most frequently used expert from the teacher MoE model, then trains the FFN modules of the student model through layer-wise distillation. CMoE distills a binary dense model from the original model using quantization techniques. Switch Transformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>)</cite> and ELSM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>)</cite> also explore distillation techniques to convert their sparse models into dense models.
Additionally, to simplify the construction of MoE models, LaDiMo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">80</a>)</cite> converts a dense model into a sparse MoE model via layer-wise distillation, where each expert learns to approximate the results of the original dense layers.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.4. </span>Expert Decomposition</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.2. Model Compression Techniques ‣ 3. Model-level Optimizations ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>-(d), low-rank decomposition is an effective method for reducing model size by decomposing a large weight matrix into smaller matrices. MPOE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>)</cite> employs the matrix product operator (MPO), a tensor decomposition technique derived from quantum many-body physics, to decompose the expert weight matrix into a central tensor and several auxiliary tensors. The central tensor retains most of the parameters and core information of the original weight matrix, while the auxiliary tensors are much smaller and serve as complements to the central tensor. After decomposition, all experts in a layer share the same central tensor, thereby significantly reducing the total number of parameters in that layer.
MC-SMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib99" title="" class="ltx_ref">99</a>)</cite> first groups the experts into several clusters and then merges each group into a single expert using a weighted sum. Low-rank decomposition is then applied to the merged experts to further reduce the model size. This approach is based on the observation that the merged experts have a lower rank compared to the original experts, making them more suitable for decomposition.
MoE-<math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>I</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib203" title="" class="ltx_ref">203</a>)</cite> identifies the importance of each expert and assigns higher ranks to more important experts while assigning lower ranks to less important ones for low-rank decomposition. The importance, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{i,j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{i,j}</annotation></semantics></math>, of the <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>-th expert in the <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th layer, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i,j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i,j}</annotation></semantics></math>, is determined by removing <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i,j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i,j}</annotation></semantics></math> and calculating the performance loss compared to the original model. The SVD rank, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{i,j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{i,j}</annotation></semantics></math>, for <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i,j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i,j}</annotation></semantics></math> is then computed as <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{i,j}=\left\lfloor\frac{(I_{i,j}+\epsilon)^{\alpha}}{\sum_{j=1}^{M_{i}}(I_{i,j}+\epsilon)^{\alpha}}\right\rfloor\cdot R_{a}\cdot M_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>⌊</mo><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>α</mi></msup><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><msubsup><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" stretchy="true">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msubsup></mstyle><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>α</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo rspace="0.055em">⌋</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{i,j}=\left\lfloor\frac{(I_{i,j}+\epsilon)^{\alpha}}{\sum_{j=1}^{M_{i}}(I_{i,j}+\epsilon)^{\alpha}}\right\rfloor\cdot R_{a}\cdot M_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> are hyperparameters, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> is the compression ratio, and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of experts in layer <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3. </span>Algorithm Improvement</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this part, we conduct an in-depth exploration of two other strategies for improving the MoE model inference algorithm.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F5.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2412.14219v2/figures/adaptive_experts.png" id="S3.F5.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:195/101;" width="195" height="101" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F5.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F5.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2412.14219v2/figures/s2d.png" id="S3.F5.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:138/102;" width="138" height="102" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F5.sf2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(b)</span> </span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>. </span><span id="S3.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Algorithm improvement on expert layers.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.1. </span>Dynamic Gating</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given the significant progress made in utilizing the sparsity of MoE models, specific strategies can be employed to further exploit this sparsity in the inference process. Due to the vertical parallel structure of MoE experts, dynamically reducing the number of experts activated for each token clearly presents an effective strategy. Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.3. Algorithm Improvement ‣ 3. Model-level Optimizations ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>-(a) illustrates the MoE layer’s calculation process after the skip mechanism is applied, in contrast to the original process.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Li <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">et al.</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">93</a>)</cite> proposes a self-adaptive gating mechanism that dynamically determines the number of experts required for each token, based on the expert probability distribution. This method enhances training efficiency while preserving the sparsity of the MoE model and further reduces training time through curriculum learning. DynMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>)</cite> introduces two innovative methods for expert activation: a top-down gating approach that enables flexible per-token expert allocation, and an adaptive mechanism that dynamically determines the number of experts needed for each token based on computational requirements.
XMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib204" title="" class="ltx_ref">204</a>)</cite> employs a strategy of using smaller, but more experts, with dynamic expert activation based on threshold values to balance computational efficiency and model performance. AdapMoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib226" title="" class="ltx_ref">226</a>)</cite> is a co-design framework aimed at improving inference efficiency on edge devices. It adaptively applies three techniques: expert activation, expert prefetching, and GPU cache allocation. The comprehensive comparison of performance and methods of these works is presented in Table <a href="#S3.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 3.3.1. Dynamic Gating ‣ 3.3. Algorithm Improvement ‣ 3. Model-level Optimizations ‣ A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. DA-MoE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>)</cite> introduces a token importance prediction method derived from attention mechanisms to guide expert allocation. By assigning experts based on token importance scores, their approach achieves strong performance on the GLUE benchmark while demonstrating effective scaling with increased expert count.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T4" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S3.T4.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
